[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: '++' reads as 'plus plus' (add twice) or as a maths symbol with no effect, and i++ inside an expression is read as 'add 1 at some later time'. In Java i++ and ++i each add exactly 1 to i immediately when evaluated; they differ only in the value the expression yields.
[1] misconception (M) -> PrePostIncrementSameValue: wrong rule: x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x. Right rule: Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.
[2] misconception (M) -> IncrementByTwo: wrong rule: i++ increases i by 2. Right rule: i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> PrePostIncrementSameValue: Applies the increment rule (LT) unevenly: uses the old value in one expression and the new value in another for the same i++, or performs the increment at the end of the loop body instead of where it is written. (here mixing in: "x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x")
[4] misconception (M) -> PostIncrementAssignsLater: wrong rule: i = i++ increases i by 1. Right rule: i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.
[5] misconception (M) -> PreIncrementBeforeLoop: wrong rule: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass. Right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.
[6] misconception (M) -> IdiomOverridesCode: wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.

[0] names_the_element (N): ++ and -- are the increment and decrement operators: shorthand that adds 1 to (or subtracts 1 from) a numeric variable.
[1] states_the_rule (S): ++ has the same effect as i = i + 1 and -- the same as i = i - 1; as statements i++ and ++i are the same, but in expressions ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): i++: fetch the value of i (that is the expression's value), then store i + 1 into i. ++i: store i + 1 into i, and the new value is the expression's value. Both happen before the rest of the enclosing expression continues.
[1] output_prediction (OP): With i = 5: x = i++ gives x = 5, i = 6; x = ++i gives x = 6, i = 6; i = i++ leaves i = 5.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One execution changes exactly one variable (i) by exactly 1 and returns its old (i++) or new (++i) value.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The usual for-loop update is i++ (shorthand for i = i + 1); as a stand-alone update statement ++i and i++ give the same loop.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Inside a larger expression the result depends on which value (old or new) the increment yields and on left-to-right evaluation, e.g. j += j++ in Exercise 1.3.6.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1 (and i += k for i = i + k), so it changes the variable's stored value.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): i++, ++i and i += 1 all add 1 to i; ++ and -- change a variable only by one and are normally used for integers, while i += k works for any amount and with any arithmetic operator (-=, *=, /=, %=).
[4] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: the update of a stepper or counter (count++ in a counter, i++ in a counted loop).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> PrePostIncrementSameValue: As a stand-alone statement, replacing i++ by ++i, i += 1 or i = i + 1 preserves behaviour; inside an expression (x = i++ vs x = ++i) the swap changes the value used by 1.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use i++ / i-- as stand-alone statements and in for-loop updates; avoid them inside larger expressions (x = ++i), as the book does, and use += for steps other than 1.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: i = i++ stores the old value back. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing i = i++ to increment: i never changes, so a loop driven by it is infinite.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: ++ and -- apply only to a variable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Applying ++ to a value that is not a variable, e.g. 5++ or (i + 1)++: compile-time error.
